summary: Defines the IP Authentication Header, which gives IP datagrams connectionless integrity and origin authentication, along with protection against replayed packets. It proves a packet came from who it says and was not changed on the way. It was replaced by RFC 4302 and RFC 4305.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a wax seal on a letter. If the seal is unbroken and has the right stamp, you know who sent it and that nobody changed what is inside.

questions: what is the ip authentication header
what is the difference between ah and esp
subtitle: How IPsec's Authentication Header proves an IP packet is genuine, unchanged and not a replay.

tldr.problem: IP datagrams can be forged or altered in transit, and a receiver has no way to know who really sent a packet or whether it was changed or replayed.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication Header (AH) adds a header carrying a security parameters index, a sequence number and an integrity check value computed with a secret key over the packet, with fields that change in transit set to zero.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2402 was a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 1826. It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4302 and RFC 4305.

facts.label: Mandatory algorithms
facts.value: HMAC with MD5, HMAC with SHA-1

today: RFC 2402 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4302 and RFC 4305, so those are the documents to read for the current specification. It replaced RFC 1826.

sections.title: What AH Provides
sections.content:
The IP Authentication Header (AH) gives IP datagrams connectionless integrity and data origin authentication, and optional protection against replays. The replay service is chosen by the receiver when a Security Association (SA) is set up. Because some IP header fields change in transit, AH protects the IP header only in a piecemeal way, and it covers upper-level protocol data fully.

AH can be used alone, together with the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), or nested through tunnel mode. It can protect traffic between two hosts, two security gateways, or a gateway and a host. ESP can provide the same services plus confidentiality, and the main difference in authentication is coverage: ESP does not protect IP header fields unless they are encapsulated by ESP in tunnel mode. The RFC assumes the reader knows the Security Architecture document (RFC 2401). Key management options are manual keying and automated keying via IKE.
sections.plainLanguage: AH is a seal that proves a letter came from the right person and was not changed. It does not hide what is written inside, though.

sections.title: The Authentication Header Format
sections.content:
The header just before AH carries the value 51 in its Protocol (IPv4) or Next Header (IPv6) field. AH itself has six mandatory fields, all included in the integrity check.

  • Next Header (8 bits) names the payload that follows.
  • Payload Len (8 bits) is the AH length in 32-bit words minus 2. For the standard 96-bit authentication value it is 4.
  • Reserved (16 bits) MUST be zero.
  • Security Parameters Index (SPI) is an arbitrary 32-bit value that, with the destination address and the protocol AH, identifies the SA. Values 1 through 255 are reserved by IANA, and zero is for local use and MUST NOT be sent on the wire.
  • Sequence Number is a 32-bit increasing counter. The sender MUST always send it, but the receiver need not act on it.
  • Authentication Data is variable length, a multiple of 32 bits, and holds the Integrity Check Value (ICV) plus any padding.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal has a label that says what comes next, how big the seal is, which secret code to use, a counting number, and finally the stamp itself.

sections.title: Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
Like ESP, AH works in two modes. In transport mode, which applies only to host implementations, AH goes after the IP header (and any IPv4 options) and before the upper layer protocol such as TCP or UDP. In IPv6, AH is treated as an end-to-end payload, so it appears after the hop-by-hop, routing and fragmentation extension headers.

In tunnel mode, an outer IP header carries the addresses of, for example, security gateways, while the inner header carries the ultimate source and destination. AH then protects the entire inner packet. When AH is implemented in a security gateway protecting transit traffic, tunnel mode must be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport mode puts the seal on the letter itself. Tunnel mode puts the whole letter in a new sealed envelope with a new address on the outside.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Packets
sections.content:
The ICV is computed over the IP header fields that are immutable or predictable on arrival, the AH header with the Authentication Data set to zero, and the upper-level data. A field that may change in transit, such as the IPv4 TTL or header checksum, is set to zero for the calculation, which keeps alignment and length fixed. Appendix A classifies IPv4 options and IPv6 extension headers the same way.

The sender starts its counter at 0 and increments it, so the first packet carries sequence number 1. With anti-replay on (the default), the sender MUST NOT send a packet that would make the counter cycle, and sets up a new SA first. IP fragmentation happens after AH processing, and a receiver MUST discard an apparent fragment, which is an auditable event, because reassembly comes before AH processing.

On receipt the SA is found from the destination address, the protocol AH and the SPI. If none exists, the packet MUST be discarded. For anti-replay, a sliding receive window is used. A minimum window size of 32 MUST be supported and 64 is preferred as the default. The window is updated only after the ICV verifies. If the computed ICV does not match the received one, the packet MUST be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender numbers each letter 1, 2, 3 and the receiver keeps a list of numbers already seen. A letter with a repeated number, a wrong stamp or a missing code is thrown away.

sections.title: Conformance, Auditing and Security
sections.content:
A conforming implementation MUST fully implement the AH syntax and processing and comply with the Security Architecture document. It MUST support two mandatory-to-implement algorithms: HMAC with MD5 and HMAC with SHA-1. Anti-replay should not be provided with manually keyed SAs, because the sender's counter state could not be recovered automatically if overflow were near. All implementations MUST support anti-replay, though the receiver may turn it off per SA.

If AH is built into a system that supports auditing, AH MUST support auditing and let an administrator enable or disable it. The RFC says no message should be sent to the apparent sender when an auditable event occurs, to avoid inducing denial of service. Its Security Considerations section is brief: security is central to the design of the protocol, and these concerns run through the whole specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who builds this must support the same two basic recipes for the stamp, so their letters can be checked by each other. Guards keep a log of bad letters but do not reply to the sender.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 1826
sections.content:
This version replaces RFC 1826. The anti-replay service became an integral, mandatory part of AH rather than a feature of a transform in another document, and a sequence number is now carried at all times. The default algorithms changed to HMAC with MD5 or SHA-1 instead of keyed MD5, for security reasons. The list of IPv4 header fields excluded from the ICV was expanded to include OFFSET and FLAGS.

The text also adds rationale, examples of AH placement for IPv4 and IPv6, clearer auditing rules, and makes tunnel mode a mandatory feature, whereas it was mentioned only in passing in RFC 1826.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of the rules. It adds a counter against copied letters, uses stronger stamps and explains more clearly where the seal goes.
